extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communicators, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and executing public relations campaigns: how to reach heterogeneous publics, choose and use established media, subdivide and appeal to overlapping groups, and craft messages based on psychology and changing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The proponent of a point of view must utilize existing avenues of approach—daily press, magazines, lecture circuits, advertising mediums, motion picture channels, radio, and other existing means for the communication of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovators and innovations cannot create their own channels in modern conditions; building independent organs (new newspapers, radio stations, motion picture distribution) is generally infeasible because of cost and time. Examples: reliance on daily press, magazine, lecture circuits; creating an independent radio station or motion picture distributing agency is likely too slow and costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide the public and present through multiple avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must sub-divide the appeal of his subject and present it through the widest possible variety of avenues to the public, reaching majorities and minorities through their respective approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze component groups closely (e.g., dentists, bankers, real estate operators) and approach each group on its strongest appeal. Use different channels and forms appropriate to each subgroup's habits and interests (e.g., museums for art-lovers, newspapers for general readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to heterogeneous and dissimilar groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Because populations are heterogeneous (no common ancestry, tradition, or cohesive intelligence), messages must be translated and adapted so they may be understood logically and emotionally by the educated and uneducated, urban and rural, laboring and professional audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing scattered or culturally diverse audiences (example: Czechoslovak immigrants), translate appeals into terms comprehensible across education, geography, and language differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage interlapping group formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of many groups whose interests overlap; the public relations counsel should utilize overlapping memberships to reach individuals through multiple group affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map individuals' multiple group identities (religion, profession, hobby, economic class) and craft appeals that will reach them via each affiliation. Example: the Metropolitan Opera horseshoe audience reached via art, music, sports, commerce, etc.; the Russian Ballet used multiple appeals (art, music, photographs) so each individual heard of it in terms of one or more group allegiances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit continuous shifting of groups and changed conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The shifting memberships of groups and changing external conditions create opportunities to modify opinions; the PR counsel must take changed physical and social conditions into account and use them to alter viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use events or technological changes (radio, automobile, airplane) to create receptivity. Example: savings bank thrift campaigns succeeded during inflation when conditions made the message timely; railroad shopmen strike increased public receptivity to government ownership of railways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize on fundamental human instincts and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract and capitalize on universal instincts (self-preservation, sex, hunger/food) and primary emotions (flight-fear, repulsion-disgust, curiosity-wonder, pugnacity-anger, self-display, self-abasement, parental-love) to craft persuasive appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete appeals: shelter (radiator ad), gustatory appeal (food ads), sex appeal (soap ads), safety/hygiene messaging (hair-net, food dispensers). Choose the instinct/emotion most likely to move the target group and frame messages accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as an impartial observer using psychological knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The PR counsel must step out of his own group to view problems impartially and apply knowledge of individual and group psychology to project clients' points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting the counsel's own group biases dictate strategy; assess the target public's 'logic-proof compartments' and herd reactions, and design messages that overcome those mental barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of persuasion and root messages in real needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is not responsible for creating or standardizing public opinion; established points of view become established by satisfying real or assumed human needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to coerce uniformity of belief. Instead, ground appeals in genuine needs or perceived benefits so the public will accept the message voluntarily rather than through forced persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use education-by-information to build cohesive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Education by information (e.g., Committee on Public Information) can be used to create common consciousness and cohesion around national aims or policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present clear information through chosen mediums to help public understanding; combine informational campaigns with other approaches to reach diverse elements of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid costly attempts to found independent mass media unnecessarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a new daily newspaper, radio station, or motion-picture-distributing agency is often economically impractical and rarely justified by results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the great capital and recurring costs of newspapers (examples of equipment and payroll) and the rarity of new papers turning profitable; prefer using existing media unless extraordinary circumstances justify creating new organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate and manage a medium's effects on public viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The PR counsel must estimate what difference a medium (e.g., radio) will produce in a section of the public and decide whether to enlarge or strengthen that medium for client advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how media change audience perceptions and habits (radio made farmers more aware of world events); adjust strategy to either accelerate adoption (if beneficial to client) or bolster the medium's prestige to help fulfill its modifying mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the greatest common factor to secure unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity among diverse groups can be secured only by finding the greatest common factor or divisor that will appeal broadly (fundamental appeals like loyalty, fairness, patriotism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select broad, fundamental appeals when the aim is to mobilize a wide and unhomogeneous audience (example: reestablishing ex-service men used loyalty and patriotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple, reinforcing appeals to reach the same individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals respond when they encounter an idea through several different appeals tied to their various group memberships; repeated exposures in different contexts reinforce the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns so that the same person meets the idea as a member of different groups (e.g., silk shown as fashion to women's clubs, as art in museums, as education in schools), increasing overall effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the economic feasibility of campaign vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the monetary and logistical difficulties of reaching and influencing large populations—consider the costs of blanket advertising, establishing lecture services, or new broadcast outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cost-benefit reasoning: blanket advertising and pamphletizing can blanket the country but at high cost; some channels may be effective only to limited extents; choose media that provide the best reach per cost for the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project ideas through prepared intermediary groups
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce new or taboo concepts, project the doctrine through groups and sections of the public that are prepared to work with the counsel (opinion leaders, intermediary organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Damaged Goods' made the American public accept the word 'syphilis' by projecting sex-hygiene doctrine through groups ready to work with the counsel. Identify and mobilize supportive groups to legitimize and diffuse sensitive ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curiosity and 'feelers' to arouse interest in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-announcements and tactics that arouse curiosity or wonder can stimulate public interest ahead of a main announcement or release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ 'feelers' and suspense-building techniques (advertising hooks such as 'What is wrong with this picture?') to prime audiences; publishers and governments use this to increase attention to forthcoming material.

rubrics_metrics.name: When appropriate, invoke pugnacity/anger to create engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity (anger) is often used by PR counsel to construct events, enact combats, and create issues that mobilize public reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adversarial framing and issue-creation judiciously to elicit engagement; be mindful that stirring anger may also polarize and have unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for group inertia and the entrenched direction of public mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The public mind often has its main direction irrevocably set; PR counsel must recognize established inertia and work with, not futilely against, the prevailing currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study historical cases (e.g., Napoleon) where leaders succeeded when moving public opinion in the direction it was already headed, and failed when attempting to reverse broad trends; align messaging with underlying public tendencies.
